unit.title: How your surroundings shape what feels normal
unit.needIt: What seems natural to you (how to queue, what is rude, what a family looks like) was set by where you grew up. Seeing that lets you question it.
unit.why: A student takes a test where two lines look different in length. Even though they are identical, the student's brain sees a difference because they grew up in a world of straight corners. This shows how our surroundings train our brains to see the world in specific ways.
unit.outcome: Recognize how your cultural background influences your automatic perceptions and moral judgments.
unit.reachesYou: You see this when you notice how your coworkers' priorities differ from yours based on where they grew up. You also feel it when you realize your personal goals are shaped by the school or community you attended.
unit.do: Observe one habit you have today and ask yourself if it is a personal choice or a result of your environment.

quiz.q: What does Nozick say about past injustices?
quiz.why: Nozick suggests that past injustices might require a more extensive state to rectify them.
quiz.quote: Past injustices, says Nozick, may be so great as to make necessary in the short run a more extensive state than the one that Nozick has been advocating in order to rectify them.

quiz.q: What does Rawls say about the social world?
quiz.why: Rawls looks for a justice that ignores aspects of the social world that seem arbitrary.
quiz.quote: Or, again, these principles express the result of leaving aside those aspects of the social world that seem arbitrary from a moral point of view.
